newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Sri Lanka plans commodities futures exchange.
newsitem.headline: Sri Lanka plans commodities futures exchange.

text.p: Sri Lanka, the world's biggest tea exporter, is considering setting up a commodities futures exchange, the head of the Indian Ocean island's markets watchdog said on Wednesday.
"We think there is potential to set up a commodities futures exchange for tea, rubber and coconut," Arittha Wikramanayake, director-general of the Securities and Exchange Commission, told Reuters.
"A very preliminary study on the feasibility of setting up a commodities exchange has been done," he said.

The study, carried out on contract to the United States Agency for International Development (USAID), recommended a further study to find out the costs, potential transaction volumes and the commitment to setting up a futures exchange.

"To proceed, we need the commitment of the industry," Wikramanayake said. "Because a commodities exchange not only needs producers and buyers but also some degree of speculation for which there's a need to create awareness."
Sri Lanka's business community had very little experience in futures and the public little awareness of speculating in futures, the report said.
Tea and rubber are sold through public auctions while the coconut market is more loosly organised.

Sri Lanka's sprawling plantations are the backbone of its economy. The tea crop is forecast to reach 250 million kg this year, up two percent from 1995, while rubber production is expected to rise by six percent to 112 million kg this year.
Sri Lanka is the world's largest tea exporter and is ranked eighth largest rubber producer in the world, down from the fourth largest in 1980.
The report said the manner in which tea and rubber prices had fluctuated in the past few years showed there was potential for futures.
Futures contracts set predetermined prices at a standardised date in the future, eliminating much of the risk for growers and providing room for speculation for investors.

"In the long run, business and investors in Sri Lanka and the economy will be at a disadvantage if they have no futures market for their products, while competitors of theirs do," said the report, a copy of which was obtained by Reuters.
Commodities market analysts said a futures exchange could reduce the power of big market players or cartels to dominate pricing.

The report said there was more scope for a futures exchange for rubber than for tea partly because rubber futures were traded elsewhere and partly because of the difficulties in establishing a uniform standard for tea that could be easily embodied in a standardised futures contract.
"Although Sri Lanka has the world's largest tea auction, it is questionable whether Sri Lanka can establish a futures market in tea," the report said.
But it suggested the tea industry study the feasibility of creating an index of tea prices that captured the value of a broad group of closely related teas created for the world's major markets.

If such an index could not be developed, it was unlikely liquid futures trading in Ceylon tea would emerge soon, the report said, adding that the idea should not be pursued if there were industry opposition.
